variants.title: Run the frame path
variants.context: A vision request crosses four boundaries: capture and admit, decode and transform, infer and associate, then decide and observe. Every admitted frame must reach a decision inside the stated deadline or be handled by an explicit drop, defer, or fallback policy.
variants.prompt: A loading-dock camera sends a frame that may contain a safety event. Put the steps in order, ending with the recorded evidence.

items.text: Record source, transform version, model version, latency, and outcome for later review.
Run the detector and suppress duplicate boxes of the same class.
Authenticate the camera, stamp the capture time, and decide whether this frame enters the bounded queue.
Decode, resize, and normalize using the color space and dimensions the model was evaluated with.
Apply the alert threshold and the dock business rules, then return or route the result.

variants.hint: Which stage is the only one that can refuse work?
variants.explanation: Admission bounds the work, the transform contract makes the tensor valid, inference produces candidates, and the decision stage owns the product action and its evidence.

variants.title: Run the frame path
variants.context: A vision request crosses four boundaries: capture and admit, decode and transform, infer and associate, then decide and observe. Every admitted frame must reach a decision inside the stated deadline or be handled by an explicit drop, defer, or fallback policy.
variants.prompt: A checkout system needs identity over time, not isolated detections. Put the steps in order for one sampled frame.

items.text: Detect objects and keep only candidates that pass the confidence policy.
Emit an idempotent track event and log the versions that produced it.
Associate each surviving detection with an existing track or start a new track.
Build the tensor with the pinned transform version attached to the frame.
Admit the sampled frame carrying its source ID, capture time, and sequence number.

variants.hint: Association needs something to associate; find what must exist first.
variants.explanation: Tracking is a stateful stage after detection, so identity work depends on an admitted frame, a valid tensor, and a filtered candidate set.

variants.title: Run the frame path
variants.context: A vision request crosses four boundaries: capture and admit, decode and transform, infer and associate, then decide and observe. Every admitted frame must reach a decision inside the stated deadline or be handled by an explicit drop, defer, or fallback policy.
variants.prompt: A camera starts repeating the same picture with fresh timestamps. Put the steps in order, ending with the containment action.

items.text: The transform stage would otherwise produce a perfectly valid tensor from stale media.
Admission checks source authentication, timestamp continuity, and frozen-frame signals.
Inference would return confident boxes for a scene that is no longer happening.
The decision stage marks the source unavailable rather than acting on stale evidence.

variants.hint: A valid tensor is not the same thing as valid evidence.
variants.explanation: Nothing downstream can tell that stale media is stale, so the source-health check belongs at admission and the containment belongs to the decision policy.

variants.title: Take the path to production
variants.context: Taking a vision path to production runs in a fixed order: profile every stage at percentiles, schedule bounded work against the deadline, define a deliberate degraded mode, then release with shadow and canary evidence and a compatible rollback.
variants.prompt: A new detector passes offline evaluation and nobody has measured capture-to-decision latency yet. Put the production steps in order.

items.text: Define the degraded mode: lower sample rate, a validated smaller profile, or routing to review.
Record decode, transform, queue, transfer, inference, post-processing, and network latency at p50, p95, and p99.
Release model, transform, and policy as one bundle behind shadow and canary evidence with rollback ready.
Schedule bounded work with per-source admission, deadline-aware micro-batches, and warm replicas.

variants.hint: You cannot bound what you have not measured.
variants.explanation: Profiling comes first because it tells you which stage the deadline is actually spent in; degraded modes and release evidence are only meaningful once the schedule is bounded.

variants.title: Take the path to production
variants.context: Taking a vision path to production runs in a fixed order: profile every stage at percentiles, schedule bounded work against the deadline, define a deliberate degraded mode, then release with shadow and canary evidence and a compatible rollback.
variants.prompt: A new site doubles the admitted frame rate and queue age starts climbing. Put the response in order.

items.text: Ship the new sampling and profile as one versioned bundle with a rollback artifact retained.
Cap queue age and apply per-source quotas so one site cannot take every batch slot.
Reduce the sampled frame rate to a level validated against the shortest event you must catch.
Profile the stages on the new site's media to see where the added time is actually spent.

variants.hint: Reaching for a smaller sample rate before measuring is a guess.
variants.explanation: The order holds under load: measure, bound the schedule, degrade deliberately against the quality contract, then release the change as evidence rather than a hotfix.

variants.title: Take the path to production
variants.context: Taking a vision path to production runs in a fixed order: profile every stage at percentiles, schedule bounded work against the deadline, define a deliberate degraded mode, then release with shadow and canary evidence and a compatible rollback.
variants.prompt: One accelerator pool is lost at peak traffic. Put the steps in order, ending with the record that allows restoring capacity.

items.text: Switch eligible traffic to the validated smaller profile once queue age still exceeds the deadline.
Narrow admission so only high-priority streams reach the remaining accelerators.
Record the degraded operating mode and the evidence needed to restore the full envelope.
Measure what the surviving pool sustains at p95 before changing any setting.

variants.hint: Degrading before measuring can leave you slower and less accurate at once.
variants.explanation: Capacity loss follows the same order as a release: profile the new reality, bound admission, degrade deliberately, then keep the operating evidence.

variants.title: Size the serving envelope
variants.context: Camera demand becomes a serving envelope in four steps. Admitted frame rate is streams times sampled frames per second. Effective demand multiplies that by a measured complexity factor. Safe capacity is per-replica throughput times the steady-state utilization target. Required replicas is effective demand divided by safe capacity, rounded up.
variants.prompt: A site runs 150 streams sampled at 8 frames per second. The measured complexity factor for this workload is 1.5. One replica sustains 300 frames per second at benchmark, and the steady-state utilization target is 60 percent. How many replicas does the plan require?
variants.hint: Two of the four numbers shrink what a replica may be counted on for.
variants.explanation: Admitted 1200 frames per second times 1.5 is 1800 effective; safe capacity is 300 times 0.6, which is 180 per replica; 1800 divided by 180 is 10.

mistakes.feedback: 6 divides by the benchmark 300 frames per second and ignores the 60 percent utilization target.
7 skips the 1.5 complexity factor and plans against the raw admitted rate of 1200 frames per second.

variants.title: Size the serving envelope
variants.context: Camera demand becomes a serving envelope in four steps. Admitted frame rate is streams times sampled frames per second. Effective demand multiplies that by a measured complexity factor. Safe capacity is per-replica throughput times the steady-state utilization target. Required replicas is effective demand divided by safe capacity, rounded up.
variants.prompt: A fleet runs 12 replicas that each sustain 360 frames per second at benchmark, with a 70 percent utilization target. Losing one zone removes 4 replicas while traffic stays constant. What sustained frame rate can the surviving fleet serve?
variants.hint: Failure capacity is the same calculation run on the replicas that are still alive.
variants.explanation: 8 surviving replicas times 360 frames per second times the 0.7 utilization target is 2016 frames per second of safe capacity.

mistakes.feedback: 3024 plans against all 12 replicas, which is the capacity you just lost.
2880 uses benchmark peak for the 8 survivors and drops the utilization target.

variants.title: Size the serving envelope
variants.context: Camera demand becomes a serving envelope in four steps. Admitted frame rate is streams times sampled frames per second. Effective demand multiplies that by a measured complexity factor. Safe capacity is per-replica throughput times the steady-state utilization target. Required replicas is effective demand divided by safe capacity, rounded up.
variants.prompt: A pool offers 1680 frames per second of safe capacity after the utilization target is applied. The workload has a complexity factor of 1.4 and every stream is sampled at 8 frames per second. How many streams can the pool admit?
variants.hint: Undo the complexity factor before you convert frames into cameras.
variants.explanation: 1680 divided by 1.4 leaves an admitted budget of 1200 frames per second, and 1200 divided by 8 frames per second per stream is 150 streams.

mistakes.feedback: 210 divides safe capacity by the sampled frame rate and never applies the 1.4 complexity factor.
1200 is the admitted frame budget in frames per second, not a count of cameras.

variants.title: Set the operating point
variants.context: A detector emits scores, not decisions. The decision policy maps scores to action, review, abstention, or rejection, and the operating point moves recall, false alerts, review load, and error cost together. A threshold calibrated on one camera mix can fail under darkness, weather, or a new installation angle.
variants.prompt: A dock detector misses about a fifth of real events. An operator proposes lowering the confidence threshold this week. What should the plan state before the change?
options: Recall is the product goal, so review staffing can stay where it is.
The extra false alerts this creates fit inside a stated review capacity budget.
Average precision improves on the offline test set after the change.
optionFeedback: More alerts arriving at unchanged staffing turns recovered events into a growing backlog, which loses them again.
Correct: a lower threshold buys recall by spending review capacity, so the budget has to be named up front.
Average precision is a curve summary and cannot tell you whether the resulting alert queue is acceptable.
variants.hint: What does the extra recall get paid for with?
variants.explanation: Threshold changes move recall, false alerts, queue load, and error cost together, so the operating point is chosen against a labeled sample and an explicit capacity budget.

variants.title: Set the operating point
variants.context: A detector emits scores, not decisions. The decision policy maps scores to action, review, abstention, or rejection, and the operating point moves recall, false alerts, review load, and error cost together. A threshold calibrated on one camera mix can fail under darkness, weather, or a new installation angle.
variants.prompt: A gate barrier opens automatically on a detection. During heavy rain one detection lands just under the acting threshold. What should the policy do?
options: Abstain on the gate action and route the uncertain event to human review.
Lower the acting threshold globally so that rain events clear it.
Act on the gate, since the score sits within a small margin of the threshold.
optionFeedback: Correct: uncertain high-risk actions abstain or escalate, while low-risk metadata can still be returned.
A global change to fix one weather condition shifts every camera's false alert rate at once.
A near miss is still below the operating point, and treating margins as passes moves the threshold without evidence.
variants.hint: Ask what this particular action costs when it is wrong.
variants.explanation: High-risk actions and low-risk metadata deserve different thresholds, and uncertain high-risk events should abstain or route to review rather than act.

variants.title: Set the operating point
variants.context: A detector emits scores, not decisions. The decision policy maps scores to action, review, abstention, or rejection, and the operating point moves recall, false alerts, review load, and error cost together. A threshold calibrated on one camera mix can fail under darkness, weather, or a new installation angle.
variants.prompt: A threshold tuned on daytime cameras is reused at a new site with night installations, and false alerts triple in the first week. What is the defensible first move?
options: Retrain the detector on the combined day and night data before touching policy.
Recalibrate the operating point on labeled data from the new site and its conditions.
Raise the global threshold until alert volume matches the original site.
optionFeedback: A new checkpoint reopens the whole bundle, and the immediate mismatch is the operating point, not the weights.
Correct: an operating point is only valid for the data distribution it was chosen on, so recalibrate on the new site.
Matching volume hides the miss rate the new site is now paying, which is the number nobody measured.
variants.hint: Which artifact was actually chosen on the old camera mix?
variants.explanation: Thresholds are calibrated on labeled, production-like data, so a new camera mix needs its own operating point before anyone changes the model.

variants.title: Give each part its own job
variants.context: The vision path is a chain of parts with distinct jobs. Each boundary owns one responsibility, each metric family answers a different question, and each failure mode has one correct first response. Naming the owner of a symptom is what keeps an incident short.
variants.prompt: Match each boundary of the vision path to the responsibility it owns.

pairs.label: Capture and admit
pairs.detail: Authenticates the source, stamps the frame, and decides what enters the bounded pipeline.

pairs.label: Decode and transform
pairs.detail: Produces the exact color space, dimensions, and normalization used during evaluation.

pairs.label: Infer and associate
pairs.detail: Runs the model, suppresses duplicate boxes, and connects observations into tracks.

pairs.label: Decide and observe
pairs.detail: Applies thresholds and business rules, then records model, latency, and outcome evidence.

variants.hint: Only one boundary is allowed to say no to work.
variants.explanation: Each boundary has a versioned contract, a latency budget, and an observable failure state, so a symptom belongs to exactly one of them.

variants.title: Give each part its own job
variants.context: The vision path is a chain of parts with distinct jobs. Each boundary owns one responsibility, each metric family answers a different question, and each failure mode has one correct first response. Naming the owner of a symptom is what keeps an incident short.
variants.prompt: Match each evaluation family to the question it answers about a deployed vision system.

pairs.label: Visual quality by slice
pairs.detail: Recall, precision, calibration, and tracking continuity for lighting, device, and rare classes.

pairs.label: Freshness percentiles
pairs.detail: Capture-to-decision latency, queue age, and how old a result is when it is consumed.

pairs.label: Capacity counters
pairs.detail: Admitted, processed, dropped, expired, and retried frames by source and model version.

pairs.label: Outcome per event
pairs.detail: Review load, false action cost, missed-event cost, and downstream product impact.

variants.hint: One family counts frames, one times them, one judges them, one prices them.
variants.explanation: These families measure different things, so a gain in one cannot cancel a regression in another during a release review.

variants.title: Give each part its own job
variants.context: The vision path is a chain of parts with distinct jobs. Each boundary owns one responsibility, each metric family answers a different question, and each failure mode has one correct first response. Naming the owner of a symptom is what keeps an incident short.
variants.prompt: Match each observed failure to its correct first response.

pairs.label: Frozen frames with fresh timestamps
pairs.detail: Mark the source unavailable rather than returning a confident result from stale media.

pairs.label: An accelerator pool disappears
pairs.detail: Stop admitting low-priority work and protect queue age for what remains.

pairs.label: A golden-tensor check fails
pairs.detail: Block the rollout and roll back model and transform together.

pairs.label: Confidence distributions shift in one slice
pairs.detail: Sample uncertain media for labeling and narrow authority until outcomes arrive.

variants.hint: Ask which stage is the first one able to see the problem at all.
variants.explanation: Every failure mode has one owning stage and one safe first action, which is why they are designed before an incident rather than during it.
